name: Imiquimod

card.summary: A prescription immune-response-modifier cream used to clear skin lesions such as genital warts, actinic keratoses and superficial basal cell carcinoma.
card.note: Prescription-only; strong local skin reactions are expected.

quick.overview:
Imiquimod is a topical cream that activates immune cells in the skin through toll-like receptor 7. Doctors prescribe it to clear sun-damage lesions (actinic keratoses), small superficial basal cell carcinomas and genital warts, which is how it improves skin appearance: by removing lesions without surgery.

It was discovered at 3M and first approved by the FDA in 1997 as Aldara. It has also been tried off-label in other conditions, including alopecia areata and lentigo maligna.
quick.how: A clinician prescribes the 5% or 3.75% cream for set periods on the affected area. Treated skin typically becomes red, crusted and sore before healing, and lesion clearance is assessed afterward.
quick.risks: Common effects are local redness, blistering, burning, itching, crusting and erosion, plus flu-like symptoms in some people. People on immunosuppressants after a transplant should not use it.

lead: Imiquimod, sold as Aldara among other brands, is a topical immune response modifier in the imidazoquinoline class. It is prescription-only in the UK, US and EU and comes in 5% and 3.75% creams.[1]

Approved uses include external genital and perianal warts, small superficial basal cell carcinomas and actinic keratoses.[1] Clearing such lesions is its appearance relevance. It has also been studied in other skin conditions, including lentigo maligna and alopecia areata.[1][2][3]
It works by activating TLR7, triggering cytokines such as interferon-alpha, IL-6 and TNF-alpha.[1]

angle.text: A dermatologist uses it to remove warts, sun-damage spots and small skin cancers without surgery, accepting a few weeks of visible irritation.

paras: The approved indications are external genital and perianal warts, superficial basal cell carcinoma and actinic keratoses.[1] Phase III genital wart trials of 3.75% cream reported clearance of 24.9% versus 9% with placebo.[1]

Imiquimod has been investigated for lentigo maligna, where phase III trials compared it with radiotherapy,[4][5] and appears in systematic reviews of pediatric alopecia areata treatments.[3] Evidence for molluscum contagiosum was negative in two large randomized trials in children.[1]
Local effects include blistering, burning, redness, dryness, itching, crusting, ulceration and swelling; systemic effects include fever, headache and fatigue.[1]
It activates toll-like receptor 7, leading to cytokine release, Langerhans cell migration and adaptive immune activation; it also acts on NK cells, macrophages and B cells.[1]

Scientists at 3M's pharmaceutical division discovered it while screening for herpes simplex inhibitors. The FDA approved Aldara in 1997 for genital warts and in 2004 for superficial basal cell carcinoma, and generics have been available since 2015.[1]

Randomized trials include phase III comparisons in lentigo maligna[4][5] and a trial comparing topical ascorbic acid with imiquimod for basal cell carcinoma.[6] A 2022 NEJM phase III trial studied treatment of anal high-grade lesions.[7]

timeline.event: First FDA approval for genital warts.[1]
FDA approval for superficial basal cell carcinoma.[1]
